current_runs.raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you is how we ourselves handled the question of those who fell under persecution and then wanted to return - because that question was ours, even if the name you are asking about is not in our pages.

When the great persecution ended, many who had given way - the lapsed, we called them - came back asking to be received [[alx.term.lapsi]]. Some in the church wanted them barred forever. Our own bishop Dionysius took the other path: he brought them back through repentance, even at the deathbed, and defended doing so [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. The boundary was real to us - we knew rival communities that also invoked Christ, and we held communion only with those we recognized [[alx.dw.one-church]]. But within that boundary, the door was held open for the repentant, not slammed shut. That much is ours to tell you. Whether the tradition you are asking about stood on one side of our boundary or the other, or was something else entire, we cannot say - their name is not in our record.

current_runs.raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition. The name Donatist carries nothing for us - no encounter, no argument, no letter exchanged. If they arose, it was beyond our years or outside our sight, and we will not invent a meeting that left no trace.

What we can tell you is how transmission worked among us, because that may touch what you are really asking. We passed ourselves on through three channels, each with its own strength and fragility [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. The teacher-student bond was the most valuable and the most breakable - the kind of seeing that changed a soul could only be handed on face to face, one person to another, across years. That line ran strong from Pantaenus through Clement to Origen, three generations, and then it broke [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. The sacramental practices - baptism, the Eucharist, the calendar - were more robust. They needed no teacher and reached everyone [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. And the Rule of Faith, and later the Creed, were the most formal: precise, portable, and brittle [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]].

What passed beyond us, what was lost, and what was transformed, we cannot see from inside our own horizon [[alx.force.transmission-ending]]. We can only tell you what we had, and how we tried to keep it.

current_runs.raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you is what we held about those whose faith failed under persecution, because that was our own wound. When the great persecutions came - under Decius, under Valerian, under Diocletian - many gave way. Some sacrificed to the gods. Some handed over the Scriptures. When peace came, the communities fought bitterly over them: could the lapsed return, and on what terms? [[alx.term.lapsi]]

Our bishop Dionysius defended bringing them back in, even at the deathbed, through repentance [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. That was the rule that held here: the door stayed open to the penitent, and the church did not demand re-baptism [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

But we know it was not that way everywhere. The arguments were fierce, and they split communities. We ourselves held that the sacraments did not depend on the minister's worthiness - the grace was Christ's, not the man's - and that repentance could restore even the lapsed [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. But whether the Donatists were part of that wider fight, or what they held and where, our own pages do not say. If you want to know about them, you will need a voice that speaks from where they were.

Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition. The Donatist dispute belongs to North Africa - Carthage and Numidia - not to us. If it touched Alexandria, our surviving sources are silent about it.

What we can tell you is how we handled our own version of the same wound: the question of those who gave way under persecution and wanted to return [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. When peace came after the great persecution, some in the church wanted to keep the lapsed out forever. The strict party said their betrayal had broken them off from Christ's body and no reconciliation was possible. Our bishop Dionysius took the other line. He brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and defended doing so in writing [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. The principle he held to was this: repentance genuinely offered opens the door again. The church's authority was to bind and loose, not to close what Christ had opened.

That was our own fight, in our own city, a generation before the Donatist controversy broke out in Africa. Whether the two struggles touched each other, or what the Donatists themselves said of their reasons, we cannot say from here. We can only show you what we did with the same hard question when it landed in our own streets.

What became of that choice in other cities, we cannot say from here.

current_runs.raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition. 

What we can tell you is how we ourselves understood the boundary between church and not-church, and how we handled those who had fallen under pressure - because that is the ground your question is standing on, even if the name you bring is not one we know.

Under the persecutions, many gave way. Some sacrificed to the gods. When peace came, the community fought bitterly over them [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. The strict party said they should stay out. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and Dionysius, our bishop, defended doing so [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. We refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

The line we drew was baptism and the rule of faith - one baptism, the apostles' teaching, communion with the churches that held the same [[alx.dw.one-church]]. We knew rival communities that also invoked Christ: Gnostic schools, and after 318, the Arian churches. The boundary was real to us - argument, exclusion from communion, and after Nicaea, harder tools [[alx.dw.one-church]]. But the lapsed were not outside the boundary. They had crossed it once, fallen, and could cross back through repentance.

That is what we held. Whether the tradition you name held the same, or something else, we cannot say.

We would rather tell you both - the patient teacher and the hard hand - than pretend we were always one.
